title: Chapter 50: The Roof Garden, Part 5 of 5: Counting Steps
html:
There was nowhere to go.
The landing was two paces across. Down was forty-four steps, sideways, on one leg, with a crutch, and it would take him a quarter of an hour, and the footsteps coming down from above were quick and light and would catch him before he had done ten. Up was the voice. And on the right were the railings and the garden and the glass doors.
So Corin did the only thing there was to do. He sat down.
He sat on the old stone seat built into the green wall, on the end where somebody had once brushed the snow off. Where Abner's father had sat on Saturdays with his pipe, while the boy did the sacks. He put the bad leg out straight in front of him across the landing, in its splints, because there was nowhere else to put it. He put the crutch against the wall. He pulled Abner's leather cap down over his eyes, and the leather cape round his shoulders, and put his shaking hands under the cape, between his knees, and held them there. And he bent his head, like a tired man, like a coal man's lad who has climbed up a stair to get out of the wind and sit down for a bit and get his breath.
The footsteps came round the corner above him.
"Forty-nine. Forty-eight. Forty-seven."
The voice was soft and quick and precise. It did not get louder as it came closer. It just got clearer. Every number set down by itself, separately, like a coin on a table.
"Forty-six. The Ministry by the fifth bell. Forty-five. The copying room until the eighth. Forty-four."
The footsteps stopped.
Corin did not look up. He could see, from under the flap of the cap, the step above the landing. And on it, a pair of shoes. Black shoes, very narrow, very polished, so polished that the gray sky was in them. And the bottom of a long black coat, without a speck on it.
There was a long silence.
"Good afternoon," said Lucian.
Corin made his voice low and rough. A coal man's voice. Abner's voice, slow, like coal going down a chute.
"Afternoon, sir."
Another silence.
Corin could feel the young man looking at him. Not the way Pallister had looked at him from the carriage, over him and past him, like a lamp-post. This was a different kind of looking. It was the way Lucian had looked at Toby's office in the autumn. Fast, and then slow. All of it, and then each thing. The cap. The cape. The black face. The leg in its splints across the landing. The crutch against the wall. The bent head.
The hands under the cape, between the knees.
Corin could not stop them shaking. He tried. He held them together so hard that the stiff gray fingers ached. They shook anyway. And he knew that the cape was moving with them. A little. Just a little.
"You're cold," said Lucian.
"Bit, sir."
"You should not sit on that stone." The soft precise voice sounded worried. Truly worried, the way a man is worried about a thing he has read in a book. "Stone takes the heat out of you. It goes up through the body, from the stone. I have read that. In a book on the care of the sick. Chapter four. On the Danger of Cold Seats." A pause. "It was correct. I checked it."
"Yes, sir."
"You should stand up. Or go home."
"Waiting for my father, sir. He's doing the coal. At the gate."
"Ah," said Lucian.
The narrow black shoes did not move.
"Cole," he said, after a moment. "The coal is Cole. Has been for thirty-one years. Two generations. The father, and now the son." Another pause, very small. "I did not know the son had a son."
Corin did not answer.
He did not know what to answer. He sat with his head bent and his black hands shaking under the leather cape and the cold of the stone going up through him, exactly as the book said, and waited for the young man in black to say something else. To say Harvester Vane. To say Bolt it, please. All three. To turn round and go back up the stair, quick and light and even, to the top, to Spire Row, to a door, to a man in a gray glove, and say There is a coal man on the Garden Steps who is not a coal man.
Lucian said nothing at all for a long time.
Then the narrow black shoes moved. Down. Onto the landing. One step, and another, past Corin's bad leg, carefully, so as not to touch it. Past the railings. Past the gap in the railings where you could see into the garden.
Lucian did not look into the garden. Corin saw that from under his cap. He saw the young man's narrow black back go past the gap in the railings, and his head did not turn at all. As if there were nothing there. As if there were a wall there, and not a garden. As if he had walked past it every Saturday for a long time and had taught himself, very carefully, not to look.
At the top of the next flight down, he stopped.
"Forty-three," he said, to himself. He took a step. "Forty-two. Forty-one. Forty."
He stopped again.
And then, to Corin's horror, he came back.
Up two steps. Onto the landing again. He stood there with his back to Corin, by the head of the stair, very straight, with the leather folder under his arm and the black book against his chest. And he said, in exactly the same soft precise voice, "Forty-four. I missed it. Forty-four is the landing. I must always count the landing. If I do not count the landing, it is wrong all the way down."
He said it to nobody. Not to Corin. To the stair.
Then he went down again.
"Forty-three. Forty-two. Forty-one. Forty."
He did not stop this time. The quick light footsteps went down the narrow stair between the two high walls, and the counting went with them, getting fainter, and fainter.
"Thirty-five. Home by the Ink Quarter. Thirty-four. The long way. Past the printers. Thirty-three. In bed by the second bell after midnight."
And then, from further down, much fainter, at the bend where the stair went narrow and steep and the snow was deep, Corin heard the counting stop again. For one breath.
"Thirty," said the soft voice, a long way below. "Mind the thirtieth step. The edge is broken. It is easy to slip on the thirtieth."
He did not know who Lucian was telling. Himself, perhaps. The stair.
Then the counting went on, and on, down and down, and got so faint that Corin could not hear the numbers any more, only the rhythm of them, soft and even, like a clock in another room. And then not even that.
Corin sat on the cold stone and shook.
He did not know how long he sat there. Not long, perhaps. It felt long. His hands would not stop. He took them out from under the cape at last and looked at them, and they were shaking just as hard as before, black, stiff, with the gray showing through the coal dust at every knuckle in little pale cracks. Mind the thirtieth step. He had slipped on the thirtieth step, coming up. He had hung on the rail by one hand, with his good foot scrabbling, and thought this is how it ends. Lucian could not have known that. Lucian had not been there. Lucian had been in the garden, by the frozen pool, telling Pallister about Sunday.
It is easy to slip on the thirtieth.
It was just a thing he said. It was just a careful man counting a stair that he went down every week, and knew by heart, every broken edge of it. That was all.
Corin did not know if he believed that.
Then, from below, he heard footsteps again. Coming up this time. Not quick and light. Uneven. A hobble. Thud and scuff, thud and scuff, the sound of somebody walking on the sides of her feet in boots three sizes too big. And breathing hard. And swearing, under the breath, in words that a girl of fourteen should not have known and Juno knew all of.
She came round the corner below the landing and saw him and stopped.
Her face was gray with cold and black with coal dust, in streaks, where she had wiped it with the back of her hand. Her three shawls were black. The boy's jacket over them was black. Her hands were black to the elbows. And round the bottoms of the huge boots, where the strips of blanket came out at the top, there was a dark wet stain coming through, spreading. Not coal. Corin knew what it was.
"Done," she said. She was out of breath. "Forty. Abner says come now." She looked up at him, and her face changed. "What's the matter? Corin. What's the matter with your hands?"
"Nothing."
"Rule one," said Juno. She had heard Lyra say it a hundred times.
Corin looked at her.
"I don't know," he said. "That's the truth. I don't know what's the matter with them." He put them back under the cape. "Did you see him? On the stair?"
"The one in black?" Juno's sharp face went sharper. "I saw him. He came down past me at the bottom, by the gate. He stopped and looked at me. And then he said one and went on." She frowned. "He was counting me, Corin. Like a step." She looked at the bottom of the stair, behind her, and back at him. "Who is he?"
"Somebody who carries the Archon's book."
"And he walks? On his own? Down a back stair?"
"Every Saturday, I think." Corin looked at the gap in the railings. At the garden, empty, with the trowel still standing up in the black earth. "He told the stair where he's going. The Ministry by the fifth bell. The copying room till the eighth. Home by the Ink Quarter. The long way, past the printers."
Juno looked at him for a long moment.
Then she grinned. A slow grin, white in her black face. The roof grin. The one she wore just before she jumped a gap she should not jump.
"The long way," she said. "Past the printers. At night." She looked down at her bleeding feet in their huge boots, and the grin did not go away. "I know every printers' yard in the Ink Quarter, Corin. Every one. I grew up on those roofs."
"I know you did."
"So?"
"So first we get down," said Corin. "And then we tell Silas he's got one day. And then we'll see."
And he took hold of the crutch, with his shaking black hand, and made his fingers close round it one by one, and stood up off the cold stone.
The Way Down
Going down was worse than going up.
Silas had warned him about that too. Down is where they fall, Vane. Everybody thinks up is the hard part. Up is only tiring. Down is where the bad leg has to go first, with all your weight behind it, and the good one can't catch you if it goes. So he went down the way Silas had told him. Sideways, with his right hand on the rail. The crutch first, onto the step below. Then the bad leg, swung out stiff and lowered, heel first, onto the step beside the crutch. Then the good leg after it. Down with the bad.
Juno went in front of him. Backward. One step below him all the way, facing up, with her black hands held out a little, ready, as if she could have caught a grown man if he fell. She could not have. They both knew it. She did it anyway.
She counted for him. Softly. The way Lucian had.
"Forty-three. Forty-two."
He did not tell her to stop.
At the thirtieth step she stopped counting, and looked down at it, and then up at him.
"The edge is broken," she said. "Here. On the outside. Look."
He looked. It was. A piece of the stone had come away at the outer edge of the step, a long time ago, and the snow had filled the gap so that you could not see it unless you knew. If you put your crutch on that edge, it would go through the snow into nothing.
He put the crutch on the inside, by the rail.
"Twenty-nine," said Juno.
It took them a long time. The light was going by the time they reached the bottom, the short gray winter light, going out of the sky between the two high walls like water going out of a basin. And when Corin came down off the last step, onto the lane, and stood by the little iron sign that said GARDEN STEPS, PUBLIC WAY, the prickle came back into his fingers at once. The lamp. Round the curve of the wall, over the arch. He could feel it turn on its hook toward him, the way a dog turns its head when it hears its name.
His hands were still shaking. The lamp did not make them shake more. That was the strange thing. It burned. It stung behind his ear. It made the bones of his fingers ache. But the shaking did not get any worse, and it did not get any better. It was not the lamp. It had never been the lamp.
Abner had the cart turned round already, facing back the way they had come, with its nose toward the arches. It was empty now, the boards bare and black, the forty sacks folded flat and piled at the back. He was sitting on the seat with the reins in his hand. He did not get down. He just looked at Corin, and at Juno's boots, and at the dark wet stain coming through at the tops of them, and his black face went very still.
"Up," he said. "Quick."
They got up. It was easier with the cart empty. Juno climbed onto the seat beside Abner, and Corin got himself onto the tail of the cart with his back to the boards and his bad leg out along them, and the crutch across his knees. The iron flap of the chute was down again. The gatehouse door was shut. There was a light in the little window now, a lamp lit against the dusk, and through it Corin could see Mister Prowse at his high desk with his pen behind his ear, reading his book.
He did not look up.
Abner clicked his tongue at the brown mare. And she leaned into the collar and went, slowly, up the lane, under the great white arch of the east wing, through the dripping tunnel, back into the dark of the cedars.
Corin looked back once.
He could see the edge of the roof of the east wing from here, high above, against the gray sky. A long line of white stone. The bare twigs of the small trees in their stone pots. The top of the little glass house, catching the last of the light. He could not see the garden. He could not see the trowel standing up in the earth, or the cushion on the path, or the little tin watering can with the daisies on it by the bench.
But there was a light now in the glass doors at the end of the garden. He could see it from the lane, very faint, a soft yellow glow along the edge of the roof. Somebody had lit the lamps in that room. The warm room. The room where she had gone in, with her hand in a gray glove.
Then the cedars closed over the lane, and it was gone.
They went down the Hill in the dusk.
Past the end of the drive, where the two white guards still stood by the black and gilded gates, and did not move. Between the stone pillars with the urns on them. Out onto the Crescent, where the gas lamps were burning all the way round the long white curve, and every window in every white house had a light in it now, and there were carriages at the doors. The Duke's Saturday. Corin saw the gold door of Marrow House shining in the lamplight like a coin, and people going in at it. Ladies in furs. Gentlemen in tall hats. Somebody laughing on the steps. He did not see Tibbs, or the grays. He had not expected to.
Abner did not slow down. He did not speed up either. A coal cart going home at the end of a Saturday, the way it had gone home every Saturday for thirty-one years.
Down past the end of Crown Walk, and the shut house, and the stone girl with her jug, gray in the dusk.
Down past the end of Velvet Street, where the black crape on the door of the Needle and Thimble was a darker shape in the dark.
Down the steep road where the shop windows had one thing in them each. Down, and down, to where they had cards in them again. GLOVES 2s. 6d.
And somewhere on the way down, Corin did not notice where, his hands stopped shaking.
He noticed afterward. They were near the bottom of Exchange Street, near the barrier, where the drum boys were lighting a brazier in the snow beside the black cart of hooks. He looked down at his hands on the crutch across his knees, in the light from the brazier, and they were still. Black and stiff and gray at the knuckles. And still.
He turned and looked back up the Hill.
You could not see the palace from here. The Hill was in the way. The tall houses were in the way, and the dark, and the smoke. You could not see the dome, or the white walls, or the roof garden on the east wing. You could just see, very high up, against the low clouds, a faint pale line going up. The spire. Going up into the clouds and lost there.
He looked at his hands again.
Still.
The drum boys at the barrier did not stop them, going down. They were busy with the brazier, and there was a different boy in front, older, bored, with his cap pushed back, and he just looked at the empty cart and at Abner's black face on the seat and waved them through. The black and white pole went up. They went under it.
And out along the river road. Over the Tanners' Bridge, humped like a cat's back. Through the old wharves, where the lamps were being lit, one by one, by a boy with a long pole, the way Corin had lit them himself, in Vespera's paint, on Tuesday night, at the Bourse. That felt like a year ago. It had been four days.
Juno, on the seat beside Abner, did not say anything the whole way.
She sat with her black hands in her lap and her huge boots hanging down, not swinging, and her sharp face turned to the dark. Once, on the bridge, Abner took one hand off the reins and put it on her shoulder, very heavily, the way you might put a hand on a dog that is shivering. She did not move away from it. He left it there all the way across the bridge.
They came round to the back lane behind Saint Bride's at the fifth bell. Old Amos's door was shut. But there was a light under it. And when Abner stopped the cart in the lane, and the brown mare stood blowing in the snow, the door opened before anybody could knock on it.
It was Oren.
He filled the low doorway. He had to stoop. He had his sword in his good hand, not in its sacking, bare, and the lamp from the passage behind him shone along the blade and on his big gray head. He looked at the cart. At Abner. At Juno on the seat. At Corin on the tail of the cart.
Then he put the sword down, very carefully, against the wall inside the door.
"All's well, sir?" he said.
Corin looked at him. At the big tired face. At the arm in its black sling.
He thought about a gray seal that could not be read, and a notice on a church door, and a pocket full of white sweets that nobody ate. He thought about Sunday, in the evening. He thought about a voice saying You'll lose your fingers, and a song stopped at the top, on the long note, and never coming down.
"No, Oren," he said. "It isn't."
The big man nodded slowly. As if that were the answer he had expected. As if it were almost a relief to hear it said out loud.
Then he came out into the lane, and bent down by the tail of the cart, and put his good arm under Corin's back.
"Ready, sir?"
"Ready."
What the Ledger Says
He told them in the side vault, under the skulls, with the lamp turned up.
He told it all. Rule one. Not the kind version. He sat on his stone bench with his bad leg out along it and his black hands in his lap, still black, because he had not let anybody wash them yet, and he told them, in order, the way Lyra had told him about her aunt's house the night before. The lady in the velvet cape who pulled her skirts aside. The drum boy with the hook, and the splint. The green carriage on the Crescent, and the smell of peppermint and grayroot, and the pink face that had looked at him like a lamp-post. The palace, enormous, and the spire going up into the clouds. The back gate. Mister Prowse, and his book. And two lads. The lamp, leaning. The Garden Steps. Forty-four of them. The thirtieth.
And then the garden.
He told them about the gravel, raked like combed hair. The box hedges. The frozen pool with the stone fish standing on its tail with ice in its mouth. The roses wrapped in sacking like hurt hands. The little tin watering can with the daisies on it.
The woman in gray.
He told them about the bulbs. About the trowel stopping against something in the earth, and her fingers bringing up a bulb with a little white root, and looking at it, and putting it back, and planting another on top of it. Silas, standing in the arch with his long arms folded, made a small sound when Corin told that part. A doctor's sound. He did not say anything.
He told them about the sweets in her apron pocket. A hundred of them. Rattling.
He told them what Pallister had said by the pool. All of it. Fifty-one. One fewer than we hoped. Blankets in every one. Hot bricks for their feet. And Lucian, with his black book. The Inquisition will collect him. On Sunday. In the evening. At the Inquisitor's own request.
Silas did not move when he heard that. He did not unfold his arms. He just stood very still in the arch, tall and thin, with his crooked spectacles catching the lamplight, and looked at Corin.
"Tomorrow," he said.
"Tomorrow."
"In the evening."
"Yes."
Silas nodded slowly. Then he looked out of the arch, down the long hall, at the pallets in the dark, and the braziers, and Mrs. Doyle's broad back bending over somebody with a cup.
"Well," he said quietly. "Then I've got a day."
And he did not say anything else about it, then or for the rest of the evening. He came into the vault instead, and knelt down on the stone floor in front of Juno, who was sitting on Oren's crate with her face set and her black hands gripping the edge of it, and began to unlace the huge boots.
Corin told the rest while he did it.
The glass doors. The gray sleeve. The long hand in a pale gray glove. Iris. The song, stopping at the top, on the long note, as if somebody had put a hand over it. Come in now, my dear. It's growing cold. You'll lose your fingers. And then the hands. His hands, on the railing, shaking so hard that the iron hummed.
And then Go.
And then Lucian, on the stair. You should not sit on that stone. Mind the thirtieth step.
When he had finished, the vault was very quiet.
Lyra had not said anything the whole time. She was sitting on the floor under the grating with her back against the wall, the way she always sat, in Gideon's thin brown jacket over her mother's gown, with the Ledger in her lap. She had held it the whole time he was away. She was still holding it. She was looking at his hands.
"Iris," she said at last.
"That's what he called her."
"I don't know anybody called Iris." She frowned. "Not on the Hill. Not anyone. I've been thinking and thinking while you talked. All the names I ever heard on the stairs at home, at Midwinter, when Mother had people." She shook her head. "There's a lady at the palace. Everybody knows there's a lady. But nobody's seen her for years. Not at the balls, not at church, not anywhere. Nobody says her name. They say her Excellency, and then they talk about something else." She looked up at him. "I don't think I ever knew it. I don't think anybody does."
"Somebody does," said Corin.
She looked at him.
"The man at the door," said Corin. "He knows it."
Nobody said anything to that.
On the crate, Juno made a sound through her teeth. Silas had got the first boot off, and was unwinding the strips of blanket from her foot, slowly, and the last strips were stuck. He wet them with warm water from a cup and peeled them back a little at a time. Under them the foot was red and swollen, and the skin had broken open along the side, where she had walked on it all day, and was bleeding. And the two smallest toes were not red. They were a dark dull purple, going black at the tips, like grapes left too long on the vine.
Silas looked at them for a long time.
"Juno," he said.
"I know."
"Do you?"
"I can see them, can't I?" Her voice was high and fierce. "I've got eyes." She stopped. She swallowed. "Are they coming off?"
"Yes."
"When?"
Silas did not answer at once. He looked at the toes. He looked out of the arch, down the long hall. He looked at his own long hands.
"Not tonight," he said. "They'll keep. Not tonight. When I can do it properly. With light, and something for the pain, and clean water." He started to wind clean linen round the foot, gently, the way he did everything. "After Midwinter."
"After Midwinter you'll be gone," said Juno.
Silas went on winding.
"Then somebody else will do it," he said.
Juno looked at the top of his head, bent over her foot. Her sharp face worked. Then she looked away, at the wall, at the skulls in their niche, and set her jaw, and did not cry. Corin watched her not cry. It was worse than watching someone cry.
When the foot was wrapped, Silas did the other one. That one was better. All five toes red, not purple. He said nothing about it. He just wrapped it, and tied it, and sat back on his heels on the stone floor.
"No boots," he said. "Not tonight. Not tomorrow. You'll walk on these, Juno, and I'll take the whole foot."
"You won't be here to take it."
"Then I'll come back from wherever they put me," said Silas, "and take it out of spite."
And Juno laughed. It came out of her like a sob. But it was a laugh.
Later, when Silas had gone back out to the long hall, and Oren was on his crate in the arch again, and Juno was asleep at last on a pallet by the wall with her wrapped feet up on a folded blanket, Lyra brought a bowl of warm water and a cloth and knelt down by the bench and began to wash Corin's hands.
She did it slowly. The coal came off black into the water, in clouds. Under it the gray came up, dull pewter gray, the same as it had been this morning. She washed each finger. She washed the backs of the hands and the palms and the wrists. She washed the knuckles, where the coal had cracked, and the gray had shown through at the railing, and the shaking had been.
The hands were still.
She dried them on the cloth. Then she held them, both of them, in her own two hands, in Madame Hesper's old gloves, and looked at them.
"Hum it," she said.
Corin looked at her.
"The song," said Lyra. "Her song. The rest of it. You said you heard it five times. Hum it for me."
"I can't sing."
"I didn't ask you to sing. I asked you to hum."
He opened his mouth to say that he did not have it. That he had heard it five times, from behind a railing, and that nobody learns a tune in five times. That it was not his. That it had never been his.
Rule one.
He shut his mouth. He looked down at his gray hands in her gloved ones.
And he hummed.
He hummed the three notes first. The ones he had heard all autumn. Pell's jar, and the busker's fiddle, and Wren. Low and rough and not very true, because he could not sing. And then he did not stop. He went on. Into the fourth note, and the fifth. The climb. He did not have to look for them. They were there. They came up out of him one after another the way the steps had come down under his crutch, each one where it should be. Up, and up. And then the long note at the top. Held. Hanging. Like a moon on a string.
And down.
Slowly. Note by note. Going down and round and home.
He stopped.
Lyra's hands had gone very tight round his.
She was not looking at him. She was looking at nothing. At the wall behind him, at the lamp, at somewhere very far away. Her face was white and perfectly still. And there were tears running down it. Not many. Two. One from each eye, slow, all the way down to her chin. She did not wipe them.
"That's it," she said. Her voice was almost not there. "That's it. That's the one. On the stairs. The one that goes up and hangs." She took a breath that shook. "I had the top of it. That was all I had left. The place where it hangs. I didn't have the going down. I didn't know it came down."
She looked at him then.
"Where did you get it, Corin?"
"In a garden. Today."
"Five times."
"Five times."
"Nobody learns a song in five times."
"No," said Corin.
She waited.
And he told her the truth. Because it was rule one. Because she had held his Ledger all day while he was away. Because he did not have anything else.
"I don't know," he said. "It didn't feel like learning. It felt like remembering. Like something I had once, a long time ago, before the Ledger. Before Malakor. Before any of it." He looked at his still gray hands. "I've looked for it all autumn. Every time I heard those three notes. I looked in every room I've got left, and it was never there. And then she hummed the rest of it, and it was." He stopped. "I don't know how that can be. I don't know what it means."
Lyra did not say anything for a long time.
Then she let go of his hands, and opened the Ledger in her lap, and turned it round, and gave it to him. Open. At a clean page, near the back, after the lists. She had found it for him. And she held out the pencil.
He took it. His fingers closed round it, one by one. They did not shake.
He wrote.
Saturday. Day ten. The Hill, in Abner Cole's coal cart.
The Archon's palace. The roof garden on the east wing, seen from the forty-fourth of the Garden Steps. Mind the thirtieth.
A woman in gray, planting bulbs on top of bulbs. A pocket full of sweets she doesn't eat. Iris. She hums all of it. The whole song. The rest of it is: up, and hang, and down, and home.
A man called her in. Gray glove. The kindest voice I ever heard. My hands shook. I do not know why. They stopped at the bottom of the Hill.
Malakor said: Go. The first word in six days. He was afraid. I have never known him afraid.
Silas: tomorrow, Sunday, in the evening. The Inquisition. By the Inquisitor's own request.
Lucian: the Ministry by the fifth bell. The copying room till the eighth. Home by the Ink Quarter, the long way, past the printers.
He stopped. He looked at it. Then, under it, he wrote one more line.
Spent today: nothing.
He looked at that line for a long time.
Then he turned to the back of the book, to the page with THOSE I OWE at the top, and under Madame Hesper. Agnes. She held her door, he wrote:
Abner Cole. Thirty-one years at that gate. He put my hands in coal and said, now you're a coal man.
Juno. Two toes. Forty sacks.
He closed the Ledger.
Lyra was looking at him.
"Tonight," she said. It was not a question. She had read the line about Lucian over his arm, upside down, the way she read everything.
"The eighth bell," said Corin. "The Ink Quarter. The long way, past the printers."
"You can't go."
"I know."
"Juno can't go. Silas said."
"I know."
"Then—"
"I don't know yet," said Corin. "But he carries the book. He carries the book that says where every paper goes, and who reads it, and who says yes. And tomorrow evening they take Silas, and on Monday morning they take fifty-one children." He put his gray hand flat on the Ledger. "And on Monday night, the box. There isn't another Saturday, Lyra. There's this one."
She looked at him a moment longer.
Then she said, very quietly, "Rule one. Don't go alone."
"I won't."
She nodded. She got up, slowly, in her mother's creased gown, and took the bowl of black water, and went out into the long hall to empty it.
Corin sat on his bench under the skulls.
Out in the long hall, the children breathed. The braziers ticked. Mrs. Doyle had stopped singing. Somewhere a cup was put down on stone.
And then, very faint, from one of the pallets near the arch, from the place where a girl of six lay with her eyes open, watching the lamp, a sound came.
It was so small that Corin thought at first he had imagined it. A breath with a shape in it. Three notes. Low and thin and not quite true. Going up, the way they always went. And then stopping, the way they always stopped.
Polly.
She had heard him. Through the arch. While he hummed for Lyra.
Corin sat very still.
The three notes came again. Thinner this time. Up, and up, and stop. And then nothing more. Just the breathing of the long hall, and the braziers, and the dark.
But she had done it. Twice. A child who had not known her own name since the autumn. Who had blinked, once, on Thursday, and looked at Lyra, and that had been the best thing in the crypt all week.
Corin opened the Ledger again, to the page he had just written. And at the bottom of it, under Spent today: nothing, in very small letters, he wrote:
Polly hummed three notes.
And then, because it was true, and because he did not know when he would be able to write it again:
Something was given back today. I don't know what. I don't know who by. But I'm writing it down so I don't forget it happened.
